title: Armies in the Trap
subtitle: The Vyazma–Bryansk encirclement operations.
author: Robert M. Dobo
summary: The Vyazma and Bryansk enclosures leave Soviet forces resisting, withdrawing and facing lethal captivity while German formations divide between containment and pursuit.
body:
What it means to close a pocket

On 7 October, German spearheads converged around Vyazma, cutting the main escape routes of major Soviet forces west of the city. Farther south, Guderian's advance and Second Army's pressure were breaking Bryansk Front into separated groups. These were immense German successes, but the enclosed forces did not surrender at the moment the roads were cut. They continued fighting, sought gaps and attempted to break through the perimeter. The attackers now had to maintain what their speed had achieved. Every formation committed to holding the enclosures was a formation less readily available for pursuit towards Moscow, while every further day of resistance gave the Soviet command time to build a defence beyond the disaster. [1][2]

The preceding study described the German plan as a set of coordinated movements. Here the plan's success created a new operational dilemma. Mobile forces could keep driving east to exploit the rupture, but a large body of Soviet troops remained on their flanks and behind them. Leave too few forces to contain those troops and corridors might reopen; leave too many and the road towards Moscow would lose the very speed for which the panzer groups had been concentrated. This was not an abstract disagreement among generals. It concerned the placement of divisions, artillery and fuel on particular roads while tens or hundreds of thousands of people fought, fled or were captured within a changing battlefield.[3][1][2]a

The two principal encirclement areas must be kept separate. The Vyazma operation turned around Soviet forces to the west of that city. The Bryansk fighting involved a more broken landscape of forests and dispersed Soviet formations farther south. Later German reports counted vast numbers of prisoners, but their totals differ between accounts and were compiled after prolonged fighting. A retrospective prisoner count cannot serve as the population of a perfectly sealed pocket on 7 October. The U.S. Army history explicitly notes that many of Eremenko's troops eventually escaped or remained in the woods and that German forces were tied down there into the third week of October. That is a reason to examine the two battles on their own terms rather than use “Vyazma–Bryansk” as one undifferentiated disaster.[1]b

Vyazma: the northern enclosure

The northern enclosure developed around Vyazma, where German mobile forces converged behind Western and Reserve Fronts. Third Panzer Group approached from the north and Erich Hoepner’s Fourth Panzer Group from the south. Their meeting cut the principal eastward routes of the Soviet armies still fighting farther west. Soviet soldiers could continue to resist or seek gaps after the operational position had been broken; closing the ring did not mean that its reduction was complete.[1][2]

The convergence isolated armies from the Soviet Western and Reserve Fronts, threatening the entire defence west of Moscow. It also created a battle along the new perimeter. Soviet units inside could concentrate against a weak point, while forces outside could try to relieve them or defend the approaches farther east. German troops had to face both possibilities. Closing the principal roads therefore began a demanding containment operation rather than completing the defeat at once. The mobile forces that had created the ring were valuable precisely because they could move quickly, but the continued Soviet resistance required some of them to remain in place and hold it. [1][3]

Closing the enclosure created competing tasks for the German mobile formations. Units moving east still relied on roads behind Soviet troops that had not surrendered. Units remaining on the perimeter had to stop escapes and protect those routes. Vyazma therefore did not immediately release the whole German force for pursuit. The resistance inside the enclosure continued to affect the battle for Moscow.[1]c

A ring has two fronts

An enclosure has an inward and an outward face: troops must contain those surrounded while protecting themselves from relief attacks. At Vyazma, German mobile formations were needed both for the perimeter and for pursuit. Closing the ring therefore created another demand on the forces expected to advance towards Moscow.[3][1]d

Bryansk: a less neat battle

The southern operation had begun two days before the main assault. By 7 October, Guderian's command had been redesignated Second Panzer Army, and its advance through the Orel direction threatened Eremenko's Bryansk Front from the east while German Second Army pressed from the west. The purpose was to divide Soviet forces into groups that could be contained and defeated. Forests and the spread of the defending formations complicated that task. German troops could seize a main route while Soviet units still moved through adjoining country, sought contact with headquarters or attempted to get east. The loss of the front's connections did not mean that all its men had ceased acting as soldiers. [1][2]

The southern battle was especially difficult to summarise because its enclosures lay on different sides of Bryansk. The German account describes Soviet formations pressed into pockets southwest and northeast of the city, with Second Army and Guderian's mobile forces sharing the work of containment. Capturing a junction could disrupt Eremenko's communications without ending the fighting throughout either enclosure. Forest tracks offered routes that did not appear as major roads on an operational map, and German forces could not occupy every interval immediately. Some Soviet troops subsequently escaped east; others remained behind the German front. The persistence of these groups made the Bryansk operation a continuing demand on German troops, rather than a completed preliminary to the march on Moscow.[1][2]e

The postwar terrain study describes Guderian’s advance through the Desna river system and wooded, marshy country. Its authors stress the need to reach firmer roads and a railway near Orel before the wet season. This helps explain the early southern start and German concern about movement. Their emphasis on terrain remains a retrospective German interpretation. Soviet resistance also caused delay, with the balance between the two varying across the battlefield.[4][1]

The southern fighting did not yield one compact enclosure that could be finished at a stroke. German forces had to maintain pressure on separated concentrations while watching the roads through which Soviet units might withdraw. Forest and marsh made movement difficult for both sides, but also complicated the task of sealing an area with troops whose numbers were finite. Escapes from the Bryansk fighting therefore coexist in the record with a major Soviet defeat. They do not cancel it, and the defeat does not justify treating every formation as destroyed on the day the main routes were cut. The battle continued as a series of attempts to contain, resist and break out. [1]

The German army also had to decide how much force to leave behind in the forests. Every battalion guarding a supply route or reducing an isolated Soviet position was a battalion unavailable for immediate pursuit. Every surviving Soviet group capable of striking a road threatened the transport of fuel, ammunition and food to the leading troops. This is how resistance could matter even when it could not reverse an encirclement. The effect was measured in the time and forces required to make the German advance safe, not only in the number of towns a surrounded formation held. The struggle at Bryansk therefore affected the pace of Typhoon long after German reports could announce a large victory.[1][4]f

Soviet choices inside the rings

Orders to Bryansk Front combined permission to withdraw with demands for further attacks. At 22:39 on 5 October, the Stavka approved movement to new lines while requiring the front to cut the Orel grouping off from its base near Glukhov and retain Bryansk and Karachev. A directive two days later again called for the Orel grouping’s destruction and a new defensive line, while insisting that rifle and cavalry divisions preserve their equipment and avoid enclosure. Withdrawal remained tied to tasks that the deteriorating situation made increasingly difficult.[9]

The 7 October directive also demanded reliable radio contact with the General Staff and subordinate armies. The requirement identifies what coordinated action needed; it does not prove that the connections existed. Headquarters still sought the destruction of an enemy grouping while soldiers inside the enclosures faced the immediate problem of getting men and weapons through a closing route. Continued resistance was real, but it was not necessarily the execution of the larger missions assigned from above.[9]g

Capture, desertion and unauthorised withdrawal describe different acts and outcomes. A soldier overrun after his formation exhausted its ammunition had not necessarily chosen to abandon it. A group moving east without contact with headquarters might be attempting to rejoin the army. Soviet security authorities nevertheless treated retreat and separation as problems of political reliability as well as military organisation. Edele's work shows why their classifications require scrutiny: the records describe both genuine desertion and soldiers detained after losing their units. The German prisoner totals cannot decide which circumstances applied to any individual. They record captives, not a collective verdict on the conduct of those captured. [5]h

Behind the pockets, rebuilding a defence required new destinations for supplies. On 7 October, the General Staff reassigned railway supply axes to Western and Reserve fronts. Western Front’s control stations included Klin, New Jerusalem and Golitsyno; Reserve Front’s arrangements ran through Naro-Fominsk, Maloyaroslavets and the Tula–Kaluga approaches. Central departments were instructed to redirect consignments. These administrative decisions could not recover the trapped armies, but they helped connect another defence to the railway network.[9]i

Numbers and the people counted

The defeat was immense, but a precise prisoner total is less secure than the familiar rounded figures suggest. The German planning history reports 658,000 captives from the two operations combined. The later U.S. Army synthesis distributes its totals differently, assigning 663,000 to Vyazma and about another 100,000 to Bryansk. Those accounts should not be added together or presented as mutually corroborating figures. They concern retrospective German counts, with boundaries and compilation dates that this evidence does not reconcile. The safe conclusion is a loss of hundreds of thousands of Soviet soldiers through capture across the October encirclements. None of those eventual totals describes a completed surrender on 7 October, when substantial forces remained in action.[2][1]j

The people behind those totals entered a system in which capture could be deadly. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum documents the systematic neglect, starvation, exposure and shootings of Soviet prisoners of war in German custody during 1941. Its account describes inadequate shelter and food, brutal marches to the rear, and very high mortality during October. These conditions were not simply the unavoidable consequence of transport difficulties, nor can a later death rate be assigned to a specific captive on 7 October. German policy and the way authorities chose to handle prisoners mattered. An operational history that ends a soldier's story at the word “captured” omits a major consequence of the encirclement battles.[6]

German custodians controlled what happened after surrender. They assigned guards, organised marches and decided whether captives received food and shelter. The difficulties of handling immense numbers did not remove that responsibility. The Holocaust Museum documents prisoners driven on foot over long distances and shot when they could no longer keep up, as well as men confined in exposed camps with grossly inadequate provisions. These practices turned the removal of soldiers from combat into a further assault on their lives. The military operation created the captive population; decisions by the authorities holding it determined that the end of resistance would not bring protection. [6]

The totals also leave gaps in the accounting of the battle. Soviet soldiers who escaped the enclosures did not necessarily return immediately to an organised formation; those killed or missing were not prisoners. Nor can the surviving German claims be added indiscriminately to figures from Soviet losses without checking how each category was defined. What is secure is the scale of the military catastrophe and the lethal system into which large numbers of captives passed. Preserving the distinction between these findings avoids turning an uncertain tally into either exaggerated precision or an excuse to minimise the defeat and the suffering that followed. [1][6]k

The Soviet orders reveal the catastrophe from inside the command system. The Stavka continued assigning attacks and demanding the preservation of divisions while trying to recover contact with them. German troops faced men still capable of fighting, even where those men could no longer act as a coordinated front. That distinction helps explain both the scale of the defeat and the forces Germany still had to commit to exploiting it.[9][1]l

The uncertain capture totals

The German prisoner totals for Vyazma and Bryansk were assembled after prolonged fighting and differ between accounts. They count captives, rather than all Soviet casualties. On 7 October, substantial forces still resisted inside the enclosures. Capture exposed those who surrendered or were taken to lethal conditions in German custody.[1][6]m

Another order in the rear

The same date also offers evidence about what German military rule meant away from the panzer spearheads. The Holocaust Museum's archival case study of the 1st Battalion, 691st Infantry Regiment, in Army Group Centre's rear area records that its commander, Major Alfred Commichau, ordered company commanders on or about 7 October to kill Jewish civilians in their respective areas. The battalion belonged to 339th Infantry Division, which had assumed rear-area security duties in September after earlier service in occupied France. The date is approximate in the source, and the villages were in occupied Belarus, not at Vyazma or Bryansk. Those qualifications matter. This was not an incident inside either pocket, but it occurred within the army group's wider occupied zone while the command celebrated its offensive.[7]

The company commanders responded differently. First Lieutenant Hermann Kuhls complied. Captain Friedrich Nöll initially hesitated, then, after receiving the order in writing, instructed First Sergeant Emil Zimber to carry out the shootings in Krucha. First Lieutenant Josef Sibille, commanding 1st Company, reportedly refused. The museum's reconstruction draws on postwar judicial evidence, including Sibille's account of the exchange with his superior. It finds no recorded punishment beyond fellow officers apparently regarding him as too soft. The differences were consequential for the civilians in their areas: a battalion commander's criminal order still passed through subordinate decisions about whether and how to execute it. [7]

Sibille's refusal was not a mutiny, nor does it establish that every German soldier everywhere could resist without consequences. It establishes a narrower and important finding: within this battalion, one commander resisted an order to murder Jews while others implemented it, and the available evidence does not show him being punished for that refusal. His case weakens an automatic explanation of participation as obedience under an unavoidable threat of death. Nöll's hesitation likewise did not prevent his company from killing. An objection that ended in delegation left the victims exposed to the same crime. Responsibility lay in the decisions taken as well as in the order received. [7]n

The prosecution of Nöll and Zimber after the war generated unusually detailed evidence about a small Wehrmacht unit's participation in murder. That evidence must still be read critically: defendants and witnesses had reasons to minimise their roles, and retrospective testimony is not a recording made at the time. The museum's study nonetheless reconstructs a chain from Commichau's order to the killings, supported by more than a general allegation against the army. It places the regular armed forces inside the history of persecution through identifiable actions. The rear of Army Group Centre was a space in which military authority could be used to organise murder while mobile formations fought farther east. [7]

The Krucha evidence also records choices below company command. Sergeant Leopold W. asked Zimber to release him from the shooting detail and was excused. Other soldiers participated, later describing reluctance, revulsion or acceptance of the order's supposed rationale. These are retrospective accounts, and aversion expressed afterwards cannot be treated as proof of resistance at the time. The distinction is central to the case. A soldier could dislike the task and still help carry it out; another could seek removal without attempting to stop the killing itself. Neither response is identical to Sibille's refusal to commit his company. The evidence reveals a range of conduct within a unit carrying out a crime, rather than a single shared motive or an undifferentiated inability to choose. [7]o

Weather, time and the road ahead

The first snow fell on the night of 6 October, according to the U.S. Army narrative, and rain and snow soon began to deteriorate the roads. On 7 October, then, weather entered a campaign already complicated by the need to contain pockets and supply advancing formations. It is too simple to say that mud abruptly saved Moscow on the day the ring closed. German troops had won a major operational battle; Soviet troops were still fighting; and the German army needed to turn that victory into a further advance before its mobility ebbed. Weather changed the cost of movement, but it did not create all the other claims on trucks, fuel and infantry.[1][8]

The geography of the pockets multiplied those claims. A panzer division holding a perimeter was stationary for a reason: Soviet forces inside might break through or threaten a route. Its tanks could not simultaneously stand guard and be the spearhead many miles farther east. Infantry needed time to arrive and take over. Prisoner columns moved back along roads that supply trucks wanted to use in the opposite direction. The physical problem of passing traffic through a few corridors was sharpened by the command problem of deciding when a pocket was sufficiently contained to release mobile formations. Stahel's description of Hoepner's limited 7 October onward movements illustrates the trade-off without asking us to endorse the commander's later complaint that a different decision would have guaranteed Moscow.[3]

The next destinations also pulled German forces away from a common concentration. Routes towards Kaluga, Gzhatsk and the capital's northern approaches offered different opportunities for exploitation. Sending armour along them could widen the Soviet crisis, but only if the forces around the pockets continued to hold. Bock's command therefore faced a choice about the order in which to use its advantage. Pursuit promised to prevent a new Soviet front from forming; reduction of the pockets promised to release the infantry and secure the rear needed for that pursuit. The army could not complete either task merely by declaring the other finished. [3][1][8]p

For the Soviet command, every day of fighting in and around the enclosures was also a day in which another defensive position might be manned, a reserve might arrive or a threatened army might withdraw from a different sector. That does not turn the destruction of the Western and Reserve Front formations into a Soviet success. It identifies the military value of delay amid defeat. A road blocked to a German column for hours mattered only in relation to what Soviet commanders could do with the hours. By 13 October, the next date in this atlas, the Mozhaisk sectors and the reorganisation of the defence west of Moscow would become the central question. The seeds of that response lay in the time created by continued resistance, even as the pockets brought terrible losses.[1]

By 7 October, the Germans had inflicted a disaster on the armies protecting Moscow, yet the destruction of those armies was still being fought over. Soviet troops inside the enclosures continued resisting and seeking escape, while forces farther east began to assemble another defence. For the attackers, holding the rings competed with the urgent desire to exploit the openings beyond them. For the captives, the military disaster led into a system of deliberate deprivation and killing. The defeat's scale is therefore measured in more than the distance between the German spearheads: it lies in the broken Soviet command structure, the contested passage east and the lives placed under the power of the occupiers. [1][7]q
